screened.arithmetic:
I ran python3 -I on the three Qwen3-30B traces (/tmp/screen-speed-0/a.py and b.py). Union of k consecutive true tokens per layer, db/story/code: k=2 12.6/12.4/12.7, k=4 19.7/18.9/20.1, k=8 29.1/27.4/30.5 (of 8k). That matches the 0.455 ratio (0.43-0.48 across traces).

1) 0.59 GB/token is the best case only: it assumes all 8 drafts are accepted (alpha = 1) and the bytes are one union for 8 tokens. Bytes per verify = 0.455 x 8 x 1.3 = 4.75 GB, whatever gets accepted. With chain acceptance alpha, expected tokens per verify are (1-alpha^8)/(1-alpha). Resulting GB per accepted token (db trace; story and code are within 0.05): alpha 0.5 gives 2.38, 0.7 gives 1.51, 0.8 gives 1.14, 0.9 gives 0.83, 1.0 gives 0.59. Against 1.3 GB plain, 1.3 is beaten only at alpha >= 0.75, and the gain is 1.6x at alpha 0.9. k=4 gives 0.94 GB at alpha 0.9. The union is measured on true consecutive tokens, so it is optimistic: a draft tree's wrong branches add experts that are not in these counts.

2) Wrong baseline and double count. The 1.3 GB/token baseline is uncached. Our best path already has an LRU, and the union saving is the same temporal locality the LRU captures (hit 0.56 at 2.1 footprints, 0.79 at 4). I simulated per-layer LRU with verify blocks of k tokens (b.py). Bytes per accepted token relative to the LRU k=1 baseline, cache = 2.1 footprints: k=4 (E=3) 1.61-1.62x worse, k=8 (E=5.7) 1.34-1.38x worse, k=8 (E=3.1) 2.7x worse. At 4 footprints: k=4 (E=3) 1.0x (no gain), k=8 (E=5.7) 1.31-1.44x worse. In no case did the union beat the cache. The cache is smaller than the k=8 union (about 29 slots per layer vs 16 slots at 2.1 footprints), so it thrashes. The ratios are given as simulated; E = tokens accepted per verify.

3) Compute bound. The 4.6 tok/s ceiling assumes decode at 55 GFLOP/s. A verify batch of 8 does 96 GFLOP, and rejected tokens waste compute. If batched MoE GEMM ran near the 311 GFLOP/s prefill rate, an alpha = 0.8 chain (E = 4.2 tokens) would give a ceiling of about 4.2/0.31 s = 13 tok/s, so the ceiling could rise. That is ordinary speculative-decoding compute amortization, not expert-major. It is also untested for batch 8: only about 2 tokens share each expert there, so GEMM efficiency is far below prefill.

4) I/O-bound arithmetic at 8 GB vs best path. Best path is 2.18 serial / 4.16 overlap tok/s. Speculation with alpha 0.8 gives about 1.1 GB/token uncached and, with the cache, no better than the LRU baseline bytes. So the multiplier is at most 1.0x.
screened.arithmetic_error:
1) The 2.2x is a best-case byte ratio at alpha = 1; at realistic alpha 0.7-0.8 it is 0.9-1.15x versus uncached.
2) Wrong baseline: it compares against the uncached 1.3 GB/token, not our LRU path, and the union saving double-counts the locality the LRU already exploits. My simulation shows bytes per token 1.3-2.7x WORSE than LRU k=1 at 2.1 and 4 footprints.
3) Rejected drafts still load experts, and the trace union uses true tokens, so wrong tree branches add more expert loads.
4) The compute ceiling is not rebuilt: the answer itself concedes 4.6 tok/s still caps the case. The 4.4-8.8 tok/s figure exceeds the 4.6 ceiling for the upper half.
5) The 4.4-8.8 tok/s range comes from multiplying 2-4 tok/s (the mmap-ish baseline) by 2.2, which mixes mmap-era rates with the byte ratio. The best path is already 2.2-4.2 tok/s.
6) Cluster claims (5x, 17x) are unsupported by any of this arithmetic.

screened.idea: Cut disk bytes per token at 8 GB by decoding k (up to 8) tokens of one sequence as a group so the union of their experts (about 45% of 8k slots at k=8) is loaded once per group, giving about 0.59 GB/token and about 2.6 tok/s. It then adds previous-layer prefetch (precision 0.55) and I/O/compute pipelining to reach about 3.5 tok/s. In practice the group of future tokens can only come from speculative or draft tokens, with a cap on group size for chat latency.
screened.claimed_multiplier: "~2.6 tok/s" from grouping (vs a 1.2 tok/s I/O ceiling, about 2.2x), "~2.1" with prefetch, "~3.5 tok/s" with pipelining. The family's claim list runs 1.27x to 7x, with a 500 outlier. Quality "unchanged".
screened.arithmetic: I ran /tmp/screen-speed-1/a.py on the three Qwen3-30B traces (first 250-300 tokens each). Mean distinct experts loaded per token, as a fraction of a one-token footprint (384), with grouped loads and no cache: k=1 1.00; k=2 0.79; k=4 0.60-0.62; k=8 0.43-0.47. This matches the 45% in the idea. The same grouping behind an LRU cache of 2.1 footprints (the 8 GB case): k=1 0.40-0.46, k=2 0.41-0.46, k=4 0.58-0.63 (a whole-group set, cache too small), k=8 0.43-0.47. At 4 footprints: k=1 0.16-0.26, k=8 0.15-0.27, no change. So the grouping gain over the baseline we already have (explicit reads + LRU) is about 1.0x. The idea's baseline of 1.3 GB/token and a 1.2 tok/s ceiling is the no-cache number. Our best path already reaches about 0.44 footprint (0.57 GB/token), so grouping's 0.46 matches the LRU hit rate and does not add to it. Both exploit the same cross-token expert overlap. Compute ceiling and drafting: with acceptance a=0.7, a group of k=8 drafts gives 3.1 accepted tokens, and the 8 drafted tokens' union is 3.7 footprints loaded, so 1.19 footprint per accepted token versus 0.44 for plain LRU, which is worse. For k=4, 2.5 accepted tokens and union 2.5 footprints give 0.98 per accepted token, which is also worse. Compute per accepted token rises 8/3.1 = 2.6x, so the compute ceiling falls from 4.57 to about 1.8 tok/s. If all 8 were accepted (not established), compute stays at 4.57 and I/O at 0.46 x 1.3 GB = 0.6 GB per token, which gives about 4 tok/s (2.4 GB/s on large reads). That is what plain LRU+overlap already gives (4.16 overlap bound). The 3.5 tok/s is 0.875x of the 4 tok/s best-path number.
screened.arithmetic_error: Wrong baseline: it compares against no-cache 1.3 GB/token and 1.56 GB/s (1 MiB reads), ignoring the cache that already captures the same temporal overlap, so the saving is double-counted (grouping and LRU both draw on the 12.6/16.3/19.6/29.1 overlap). It assumes all 8 grouped tokens are accepted, but the group can only be formed from drafts, and rejected drafts still load experts. It ignores the compute ceiling of 4.57 tok/s (it restates it as headroom), the draft model's own cost and RAM (a draft model also needs resident bytes at 8 GB), and the extra compute per accepted token. It applies the 0.55 precision as if it were coverage, and it ignores the cache-size limit: the k=8 union is 3.7 footprints (about 4.8 GB), larger than the 2.7 GB cache, so reuse across groups is lost.

It only changes prefill/TTFT. Decode stays at the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling, and the output is unchanged because only execution order moves.
screened.claimed_multiplier: "2.0x to 500x" across 16 runs, including 270 s -> 29 s (about 9x) on prefill. It is stated as prefill-only: "decode stays compute-bound at 4.6 tok/s".
screened.arithmetic:
What I ran: the union of experts touched per layer over windows of W consecutive decode tokens in the three Qwen3-30B traces (128 experts per layer). This is a proxy, because real prefill traces do not exist. Fraction of experts touched: W=16: 0.28-0.33. W=64: 0.43-0.52. W=128: 0.52-0.61 (db 0.524, story 0.523, code 0.614). The traces have only 249-299 tokens, so W=256 gave 0.60 for db and W=500 cannot be measured. A 500-token prompt on the 125B (512 experts, top-10, 5000 picks per layer) will likely touch about 75-95% of experts, which is about 50-65 GB, not exactly 69 GB.
Prefill time:
- Bytes: 50-69 GB at 2.4 GB/s (4 MiB reads) = 21-29 s. At the real 0.9 MB tensor size (1.56 GB/s) = 32-44 s.
- Compute: 500 tokens x 12 GFLOP = 6 TFLOP. At the measured 311 GFLOP/s that is 19 s. With full overlap TTFT is max(19, 32-44) = about 32-44 s. Without overlap it is 51-63 s.
- Baseline, mmap with the batch already grouped by expert: the union of 50-69 GB at 0.34 GB/s = 150-200 s. TTFT gain is therefore 3.5-6x vs mmap, not 9x.
- Baseline, our best path (explicit large reads + LRU), also reads each layer's expert union once: 1.0x. llama.cpp's mul_mat_id with ubatch 512 already processes tokens per expert, so "sorting" is not new work. The only real change is the read size, the same 0.34 -> 1.56-2.4 GB/s lever as decode.
Tok/s multiplier: 1.0x on decode. On an end-to-end run of 500 prompt + 200 generated tokens at about 2 tok/s, wall time goes from about 200 + 100 s to about 40 + 100 s, so about 2.1x end-to-end vs mmap and about 1x vs best path.
screened.arithmetic_error:
- Wrong baseline: the 650 GB figure (500 x 1.3 GB) assumes per-token loads with no sharing across the batch. A batched prefill never does that, so it overstates the baseline by about 10x. Only 50-69 GB needs reading in any scheme.
- Wrong read rate: "69 GB / 2.4 GB/s = 29 s" uses the 4 MiB rate, but experts are about 0.9 MB tensors (1.56 GB/s at 1 MiB, about 44 s) unless the file is re-laid-out. It also assumes the union is exactly 69 GB.
- Ignored bounds: the compute ceiling for prefill (19 s at 311 GFLOP/s) and the resident dense 1.9 GB are not counted. TTFT also includes the first decode token.
- Not a tok/s gain: decode is untouched, so the family's "several x tokens/s" goal is not met by this idea.
- Cross-layer ordering is not a free choice. It needs a layer-major loop, which prefill already has.
- Rejected drafts: none apply.

screened.arithmetic: Compute: the 6B active parameters are not mostly experts. 12 GFLOP/token = 2 x 6B. Expert bytes per token are 1.3 GB at about 4.3 bpw, which is about 2.4B params. The resident dense part is 1.9 GB, about 3.5B params. So experts are about 40% of the FLOPs and dense about 60%. Dropping 4 of 10 experts removes 0.4 x 2.4B = 0.96B, or 16% of the FLOPs (not 40%). The ceiling goes 4.57 -> about 5.4 tok/s (1.18x), not 7.6. Bytes (my LRU replay on the 3 Qwen3-30B traces, python3 -I, scripts in /tmp/screen-speed-3/b.py, top-6 = first 6 ids of each record, which assumes the trace is gate-sorted): at an equal cache of 24 entries per layer, K=8 misses 122.8 / 103.1 / 136.6 slices per token (db/story/code) and K=6 (cache = 4 x 6) misses 80.6 / 69.4 / 93.3. That is 1.52x / 1.49x / 1.46x fewer misses. Hit rate per footprint is worse for K=6 (k=2: 0.497 vs 0.550), so the gain is about 1.5x, not the 1.33x slice-count ratio alone. Requantising to 2.5 bpw makes each slice 1.7x smaller and fits 1.7x more slices in RAM. screened.arithmetic:
Re-ran the k-union on our 3 traces (python3 -I, trace_tools.parse): unique experts per layer for k=2 is 12.67 (db), 12.61 (story) and 12.71 (code); for k=3 it is 16.46, 15.91 and 16.67. These match the 12.6 and 16.3 facts, so bytes per forward at k=2 are 1.58x (12.6/8). The mechanics hold, but there are four problems.
1) The size is not 34 GB. Q2_K is about 2.6 bpw, so 69 x 2.6/4.3 = about 42 GB. A mixed 2/3/4 map averages about 3 bpw, which gives about 48 GB. Only IQ2_XXS-class quality (about 2.06 bpw) reaches 33-34 GB, and that has the worst accuracy. At 32 GB the OS plus 1.9 GB of dense weights leave about 26 GB of cache, so it does not all fit.
2) The baseline is wrong. Our best path (explicit 4 MiB reads plus LRU) already gives hit 0.95 at 7.5 footprints (LRU table: 1.0 gives 0.31, 2.0 gives 0.55, 4.0 gives 0.79, 7.5 gives 0.95). At 32 GB the cache is about 20 footprints of 1.3 GB, so the 4-bit path is already about 4.3-4.5 tok/s, close to the 4.57 ceiling. The "2-4 tok/s I/O-bound" baseline is plain mmap, not our best path.
3) 2-bit cannot beat the compute ceiling. Dequant FLOPs are about the same, so the cap stays 4.57 tok/s.
4) The speculative double count: "~2 accepted tokens per forward" counts every draft as accepted. Realistic acceptance is 0.6-0.7, so about 1.6-1.7 tokens per forward before the draft cost. There is also no draft model. In the compute-bound regime a k=2 forward costs about 2x the FLOPs, so it only helps if batching raises GFLOP/s. Prefill ran at 311 vs decode at 55 GFLOP/s, so some headroom exists, but it is unmeasured for k=2. At 8-16 GB the 1.58x bytes also push I/O back up.
Recompute for 2.6 bpw experts (0.79 GB per token footprint, 4 MiB reads at 2.4 GB/s) against our 4-bit explicit+LRU path:
- 8 GB: about 4.5 GB cache is 5.7 footprints, hit about 0.88, disk 0.095 GB, 0.04 s. Serial gives 1/(0.04+0.219) = 3.9 tok/s vs 2.18 (1.8x). Overlap gives 4.5 vs 4.16 (1.1x).
- 16 GB: 4-bit about 4.2, 2-bit about 4.5 (1.07x).
- 32 GB: about 1.0x.
Against plain mmap at 8 GB (0.53 serial) the same path gives about 7x, but that gain is read size, which is already counted in our path. Spec decoding adds at most about 1.2-1.4x, and only with a draft model and an unmeasured batching gain.
screened.arithmetic_error: Baseline error: the gain is measured against mmap or an I/O-bound 2-4 tok/s, not against explicit reads plus LRU, which is already near the cap at 16 GB and above. Size error: 34 GB needs about 2.1 bpw (IQ2-class); realistic 2/3/4 mixes are 42-48 GB, so it does not fit in 32 GB. Double count: the 2-bit gain and the read-size gain are the same I/O reduction. Spec decoding assumes 2 accepted tokens per forward with no rejected drafts and no draft cost. The stated 4.6 tok/s compute bound caps the answer at 1.0x for 2-bit alone once I/O is hidden. Also, the accuracy cost of 2-bit is acknowledged but not priced.

screened.idea: Pin about 24.5% of expert slices (26 GB) resident and add a bias to the router logits so that about half of each token's 10 experts come from the pinned set. This cuts disk reads from 1.3 GB to about 0.65 GB per token and moves decode toward the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling. It is cache-aware routing with a static pin set instead of a dynamic cache.
screened.claimed_multiplier: Claims list 1.5x to 7x; the idea text itself says "expect 1.15-2.3x, not 3x" and "~2x headroom toward the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling". Success criterion: at least 1.8x tok/s at no more than 2% perplexity rise.
screened.arithmetic: Traces: 30B, 48 layers x 128 experts, 3 prompts. Python3 -I in /tmp/screen-speed-8/a.py: pin set learned on the other two prompts (cross-prompt), scored on the third. The natural hit rate of a pinned set is 0.159 at 7% pinned, 0.386 at 17%, 0.528 at 24.5% and 0.725 at 40%. Optimistic bias model: the m lowest-ranked misses of each token-layer are swapped for pinned experts; the router scores are not in the trace, so this assumes a good pinned substitute always exists. With m=2 the hit rate is 0.41 / 0.63 / 0.76 / 0.90 at those pin sizes; with m=4 it is 0.66 / 0.84 / 0.92 / 0.98. The 24.5% pin with a two-expert swap already gives 0.76, so "half the experts from the pinned set" is an under-estimate of what a bias could force, but that makes the quality risk larger. Throughput model: bytes = (1-hit) x 1.3 GB, 2.4 GB/s disk, compute 1/4.57 s. Best-path baseline (explicit reads + LRU, hit 0.56 at 2.1 footprints): serial 2.19, overlap 4.2 tok/s. Hit 0.78: serial 2.96, overlap 4.57. Hit 0.90: serial 3.66, overlap 4.57. Hit 0.95: serial 4.07, overlap 4.57. The 24.5% pin needs 26 GB of RAM. On an 8 GB machine only about 3-5 GB are free for experts, which is 4-7% of slices, so the 24.5% pin does not fit there.
screened.arithmetic_error: 1) It uses a baseline of plain LRU with previous-token prefetch, not our best path. Our own best path (4 MiB reads + LRU) already reaches 4.2 tok/s overlap at 8 GB, so a "2x headroom" is measured against the wrong base. 2) The 26 GB budget only exists on a 32 GB machine, where LRU with about 20 footprints already has hit 0.95 or more and is compute-bound, so there is nothing left to gain. 3) The target machines are small-RAM PCs, but the idea assumes a desktop budget. 4) The step from 0.65 GB/token to 4.6 tok/s is assumed; at 2.4 GB/s it is 0.27 s I/O + 0.22 s compute = 2.0 tok/s serial, and only overlap reaches 4.6. The overlap is not implemented. 5) The compute ceiling of 4.57 tok/s bounds the best case, so the ceiling on gain over the best path is 4.57/4.2 = 1.09x with overlap, or 1.35x serial at hit 0.78. 6) A pinned set is a static pin, and a dynamic LRU with a bias (the published method) beats it at equal RAM. 7) Hot-set transfer across prompts is only 5-21% in our notes, but with 24.5% pinned the cross-prompt hit here is 0.53 (30B, 3 prompts, so a small sample).

Against plain mmap (0.53 serial / 0.59 overlap) the total is 4-7x, but that comes from read size, not from the bias.
real_multiplier.gb16_laptop: About 1.0-1.1x over our best path. LRU with 12 GB (about 9 footprints) is already near hit 0.9-0.95 and near the compute ceiling (serial 3.7-4.1 tok/s). Bias can add at most 4.57/4.1 = 1.1x.
real_multiplier.gb32_desktop: About 1.0x. LRU is already at or near the 4.57 tok/s ceiling; the 26 GB pin cannot beat it.
real_multiplier.bound: Compute ceiling 4.57 tok/s (55 GFLOP/s over 12 GFLOP per token); bias can only reduce the I/O part. Quality loss grows with the share of experts forced.
real_multiplier.vs: Our best path (explicit 4 MiB reads + LRU). Against plain mmap the whole 4-7x at 8 GB is from read size.

screened.idea: Run prefill expert-major: for each layer, sort the ~500 prompt positions by routed expert and read each expert slice once, applying it to all its positions, so first-token I/O drops from a claimed 650 GB (per-token loading) to about 69 GB (29 s at 2.4 GB/s). It admits that compute (6 TFLOP at 55 GFLOP/s = 109 s) then binds at about 2.5x, and hand-waves a lossy draft or early-exit prefill to go further.
screened.claimed_multiplier: "cuts I/O (650GB to ~69GB, 271s to 29s)... compute then binds at ~109s ... only ~2.5x"; claims in the family range 2 to 500.
screened.arithmetic: Recomputed. (1) Compute: 500 tokens x 12 GFLOP = 6 TFLOP. The idea divides by 55 GFLOP/s (the decode ceiling, memory-bound GEMV) to get 109 s. Our measured prefill (batched GEMM) is about 311 GFLOP/s on OLMoE, so 6e12/311e9 = 19.3 s. The compute bound is about 19 s, not 109 s, and the 'compute binds, so only 2.5x' conclusion is wrong. (2) I/O: 69 GB / 2.4 GB/s = 28.8 s, and that assumes 100% expert coverage. In 4 MiB reads the real number is fewer bytes: on our decode traces (Qwen3-30B, 128 experts, top-8) the unique experts per layer over the first 249-299 tokens are 0.55 / 0.62 / 0.70 (story/db/code) of all experts, and over 128 tokens 0.52-0.61. A 500-token prompt on 512 experts / top-10 is plausibly 0.7-0.95 coverage (independent-uniform would give 1.0; skew lowers it), so about 48-65 GB, 20-27 s. Decode traces are not prefill routing, so this is a proxy and not measured. (3) Bound: max(I/O 29 s, compute 19 s) = about 29 s overlapped, or 48 s serial. (4) Baseline: the '650 GB / 271 s' is a straw man (per-token loading, 500 x 1.3 GB). llama.cpp already runs prefill in ubatches of 512 and its MUL_MAT_ID groups tokens by expert within a layer, so the stock path is already expert-major: every expert is touched once per layer per ubatch, about 69 GB total. The only real difference between plain mmap and our path is the read rate and overlap. Plain mmap at 0.34 GB/s: 69/0.34 = 203 s I/O plus 19 s compute = about 222 s. Explicit 4 MiB reads, overlapped: about 29 s, which is 7.6x vs mmap (serial 48 s, 4.6x). Versus our best path (explicit large reads + LRU) the gain is about 1.0x, because that path with a batch of 500 already reads each expert once. Whether mmap sequential faulting in expert order reaches more than 0.34 GB/s in prefill is unmeasured; if it reaches 1 GB/s the gain over mmap is only about 2.4x.
screened.arithmetic_error: (a) Wrong compute rate: uses the 55 GFLOP/s decode ceiling for prefill, which runs about 5.7x faster (311 GFLOP/s measured), so the 109 s floor is really about 19 s. (b) Straw-man baseline: 650 GB / 271 s assumes per-token expert loading, which llama.cpp does not do in prefill (ubatch 512 groups by expert), so the 'cut' from 650 to 69 GB is already in stock llama.cpp. (c) Ignored bound: once compute is 19 s, the 2.4 GB/s disk rate (29 s) binds, and it cannot be improved by sorting. (d) Coverage 100% assumed, unverified. (e) Mixes TTFT with the decode tokens/s goal: prefill happens once, so it does not raise steady tokens/s, and a longer prompt only grows compute (1500 tokens = 58 s compute vs the same 29 s I/O). The draft/early-exit FLOP cut is lossy and unquantified.

real_multiplier.gb8_laptop: TTFT for a 500-token prompt vs plain mmap: about 222 s -> 29-48 s = 4.6-7.6x (only if stock mmap really runs at 0.34 GB/s in prefill; if it gets about 1 GB/s, then about 2.4-3x). It is a one-off TTFT gain and gives no steady tokens/s gain.
real_multiplier.gb16_laptop: Same as 8 GB (about 4.6-7.6x vs mmap): a layer-sweep streams 69 GB once, and extra RAM only holds one layer's experts (about 1.4 GB), so the cache helps little in the first pass. A small benefit comes from handing the last layers' experts to decode.
real_multiplier.gb32_desktop: Same I/O (a first sweep over about 69 GB cannot be cached; the file is bigger than RAM, and LRU thrashes on a cyclic layer sweep). About 4.6-7.6x vs mmap only if mmap is slow; roughly 1.0x vs our explicit-read path.
real_multiplier.bound: Disk rate: 69 GB (or about 48-65 GB at partial coverage) / 2.4 GB/s = 20-29 s; compute 19 s at 311 GFLOP/s; the true floor is about 29 s for 500 tokens and compute-bound above about 750 tokens.
real_multiplier.vs: Plain mmap for the 4.6-7.6x figures (a read-size effect, not an expert-major effect). Versus our best path (explicit large reads + LRU, already batch-grouped by expert): about 1.0x.

screened.arithmetic:
I ran /tmp/screen-speed-10/a.py on the three Qwen3-30B traces (48 layers x 128 experts, 384 accesses per token, 249-299 tokens each). It learns the hot set from the first W decode tokens, which is a proxy because we have no prefill trace. It scores the rest of the trace against a pin of the same size, against LRU of the same size, and against half pin plus half LRU.

Hit rates, W=64. Values are db / story / code, same capacity:
- 10% share (1.6 footprints): pin 0.41 / 0.50 / 0.37, LRU 0.48 / 0.52 / 0.47, hybrid 0.44 / 0.56 / 0.43.
- 20% share (3.2 footprints): pin 0.67 / 0.73 / 0.60, LRU 0.71 / 0.78 / 0.68.
- 36% share (5.8 footprints, equal to 24 GB of 69 GB): pin 0.87 / 0.92 / 0.81, LRU 0.92 / 0.94 / 0.89, hybrid 0.93 / 0.96 / 0.89.
- W=16 is worse: pin 0.81 / 0.81 / 0.75 at 36%.
- At 6% (below one footprint), pin gets 0.27 / 0.37 / 0.27. Strict LRU gets 0 there, but that is a below-one-footprint cliff, not a real option.

The 40% hit figure is not the 36%-share figure. 40% is what a 10% pin delivers (0.37-0.50), and a 10% pin is only ~7 GB of the 125B, not 24 GB. The idea mixes these up: 24 GB / 2.7 MB = 8.9k experts = 185 per layer (36%). The "69/512" and the 0.9 MB slice size in the idea are wrong, as the gap list says.

Throughput, 125B target. Disk bytes per token = (1-h) x 1.3 GB at 2.4 GB/s. Serial = 1/(io + 0.219 s), overlap = min(4.57, rate/bytes).
- Claimed h=0.40: 0.78 GB gives io 0.325 s, so serial 1.84, overlap 3.08 tok/s.
- Plain-LRU 32 GB: h about 0.93-0.95 (k of 7.5 or more footprints gives 0.95), so 0.07-0.09 GB. Serial about 3.9-4.0, overlap 4.57 (the compute wall).
- Pinned 32 GB: h about 0.81-0.92, so 0.10-0.25 GB. Serial about 3.1-3.7.
- The plain-mmap 32 GB row is 1.3 GB x 0.07 / 0.34 GB/s = 0.27 s io, so serial about 2.0. The gain over mmap comes from read size and LRU, not from pinning.
- Corrected 8 GB row from FEED: mmap LRU 0.53 / 0.59; explicit reads plus LRU 2.18 / 4.16; explicit plus pinned-by-share (hit 0.26) 1.61 / 2.48.
screened.arithmetic_error:
1. Wrong share: 40% reuse is quoted for a 6-10% pinned set but applied to a 24 GB (36%) set; the idea's own "69/512 = 13.5%" contradicts it.
2. Wrong baseline: it is compared with raw 1.3 GB per token, i.e. no cache at all. The real baseline is explicit 4 MiB reads plus LRU, which already reaches hit 0.56 at 8 GB and about 0.93 at 24 GB, so pinning starts from a higher hit rate than the 0.40 it claims.
3. Ignored bound: compute caps at 4.57 tok/s, and "4x" cannot be reached with one NVMe. The 3x depends on a second NVMe, which is a separate lever.
4. Resident bytes: 24 GB pinned plus 1.9 GB dense plus OS leaves ~4 GB for streaming misses on a 32 GB machine, and the pinned set does not exist on 8 or 16 GB machines.
5. Hit-rate source: the 35-42% same-prompt number is in-sample. Out of sample with a 16-token window, pin is 0.27 / 0.44 at 5% / 10% (FEED), and cross-prompt hot lists give 0.05-0.21.
6. Pin is below same-size LRU in every cell at 1.6 footprints or more: 0.37-0.50 against 0.47-0.52 at 10%, and 0.81-0.92 against 0.89-0.94 at 36%. A static pin adds nothing and stops adapting.
7. Prefill: it needs the prefill to reveal the decode hot set. Prefill touches most experts (~65 GB first-token load), so the "prefill-loaded" set is almost everything and only counts or gate scores can rank it. That prefill-to-decode correlation is unmeasured on our side, and ELDR says only that it is strong on Qwen3-30B-A3B.

real_multiplier.gb16_laptop: About 1.0x (0.9-1.0). ~11 GB of cache is 8+ footprints. LRU is already at about 0.95, so pin cannot add; a 4 MiB read rate sets the rest.
real_multiplier.gb32_desktop: About 1.0x (0.85-1.0) against the best path. Both sit near the 4.57 compute wall (serial about 3.1-3.9). Against plain mmap the whole path is about 2x, again from reads and LRU.

real_multiplier.vs: Our best path (explicit 4 MiB reads plus LRU). Against plain mmap its only real gain is the read-size effect, which it does not own.

screened.arithmetic:
I ran python3 -I on the three qwen3-30b traces. These are decode traces, top-8 of 128 experts, 48 layers. The k=4 case takes the first 4 listed ids, which is a proxy because I do not know whether the order is gate-weight order. Mean unique experts per layer in a window of W consecutive tokens, k=8 / k=4:
- db: W=16 43.2 / 28.2; W=64 60.5 / 42.0
- story: W=16 36.6 / 24.1; W=64 62.5 / 47.0
- code: W=16 43.2 / 27.0; W=64 69.4 / 49.1

At W=500 the union goes to about 100+ of 128 (extrapolated from the W=16 to W=64 growth; the traces are shorter than 500 tokens), so both settings read nearly the whole 69 GB. Prefill is a one-pass sweep, so bytes are about 69 GB x union fraction, not tokens x 1.3 GB. I/O is 69/2.4 = 29 s at k=10 and about 25 s or more at k=4, about 1.1-1.2x.
Prefill compute is also a bound: 500 tok x 12 GFLOP = 6 TFLOP. At 311 GFLOP/s that is about 19 s. With the dense part about 3.5B params and the active experts about 2.4B, k=4 cuts FLOPs by about 25%, so compute is about 14 s. Prefill time is then max(I/O 25, compute 14) = about 25 s against 29 s, or 1.15x, not 2.6x.

A prefill-only cap does not change decode at all; decode speed gains need k=4 in decode too. If that is applied, then at 8 GB the footprint shrinks 2.5x, hit rises from 0.56 to about 0.85, and serial tok/s is about 1/(0.033+0.167) = 4.5 against 2.18 (about 2x). The overlap bound is 6 against 4.16 (about 1.4x).

A decode k=4 gets about 1.3x on compute (ceiling 4.6 to about 6) and the rest comes from a higher hit rate. The 5-10 tok/s figure is above even the k=4 compute ceiling of about 6. 4) The quality cost is stated as "a few points" without evidence. screened.idea: Add a discrete GPU as a resident tier: ~1.9 GB dense plus about 20 GB of hot experts live in VRAM, the rest streams from NVMe. The GPU is meant to do two jobs: cut disk bytes per token (the cache) and lift the 4.57 tok/s CPU compute ceiling (the FLOPS). The brainstorm baseline is striping two NVMes (about 4.8 GB/s, 3.7 tok/s I/O bound).

The 0.9 MB slice is a unit error: an expert is 3 tensors, about 2.7 MB. Corrected: 278 x 2.7 MB = 0.75 GB, at 1.56 GB/s = 0.48 s = 2.1 tok/s serial. That matches the lower claim of 2.2, not 6.2. The 42% is the previous-token reuse, not the hit rate of a 20 GB cache. Measured LRU hit at 29% of experts (20 GB of 69): same-prompt 0.855/0.884/0.809 (db/story/code); warm from a different prompt 0.889/0.815/0.861; pinned hot list learned on another prompt only 0.57/0.44/0.70. So 42% is too pessimistic for LRU but right for static pins. With LRU hit 0.85: 0.15 x 1.3 GB = 0.195 GB/token, at 2.4 GB/s = 0.081 s, so an I/O bound of ~12 tok/s. Caveats: traces are only 249-299 tokens (cold misses are diluted), the 30B has 128 experts/layer vs 512 for the target (sparser, so hits are probably lower), and the cliff means hit is ~0 below 1 footprint. Other cache sizes (hit, I/O only at 2.4 GB/s): 8 GB cache hit 0.52-0.56, 0.6 GB/token, 4 tok/s; 12 GB hit 0.62-0.70; 16 GB hit 0.71-0.81. A 6 GB VRAM cache (4 GB sim row hits 0.0, the cliff, because 4 GB < 1 footprint on the scaled geometry) gives hit ~0 to 0.2, about 1.0-1.3 GB/token, 2.0-2.3 tok/s, equal to our explicit-read+LRU path (2.18 serial). The compute ceiling does lift on GPU: batch-1 GEMV is memory-bound, 6 GB active at ~300 GB/s VRAM is ~20 ms, and the CPU only computes the ~15% of misses (1.8 GFLOP, trivial). So the ceiling stops binding and I/O decides.
screened.arithmetic_error: (1) Slice size 0.9 MB instead of 2.7 MB, a 3x understatement of bytes (6.2 tok/s becomes 2.1). (2) 42% previous-token reuse used as the 20 GB cache hit rate. (3) The baseline is NVMe striping at 4.8 GB/s, not our best path (explicit 4 MiB reads + LRU in RAM), so the gain is not isolated: a 20 GB cache in host RAM gives the same hit rate; VRAM only adds the compute lift. (4) 1.56 GB/s used for reads when 4 MiB reads reach 2.4 GB/s. (5) Hardware inconsistency: a 'small GPU' has 8-12 GB, not 22 GB. The target is small-RAM PCs, and a 24 GB GPU costs more than the PC. screened.verdict_reason: The idea is known and shipped, the brainstorm arithmetic has a 3x byte error, and the multiplier comes from cache capacity (equally available in host RAM) plus a GPU-only lift of the 4.57 compute ceiling. Fold it into the project as an optional 'if a GPU is present' path using llama.cpp's existing flags on top of explicit-read + LRU, not as a new method.

screened.idea: Cut TTFT (prefill) by lowering active experts per token from top-10 to about top-4 (training-free, runtime override) and moving the 1.9 GB dense/attention part to the idle 12 GB GPU. It argues prefill is compute-bound at 55 GFLOP/s (500 tok x 12 GFLOP = 6 TFLOP = 109 s) and both levers cut that floor about 3x. The text itself concedes only 2-3x and +0.3-0.8 perplexity.
screened.claimed_multiplier: "Realistic combined gain ~2-3x, not 5x"; top-10->top-4 "~1.8-2.2x" on prefill; rated 38 with claims 2.2-5.0.
screened.arithmetic: (1) Wrong baseline: 55 GFLOP/s is the decode figure; measured prefill is about 311 GFLOP/s on OLMoE, so 6 TFLOP is about 19 s, not 109 s. (2) Prefill is I/O-bound, not compute-bound, on a small-RAM disk setup: P(expert touched in 500 tokens) = 1-(1-10/512)^500 = 1.00 for top-10 and 1-(1-4/512)^500 = 0.98 for top-4, so about all 69 GB must be read either way: 69/2.4 = 29 s at best (more at mmap rates, 0.34 GB/s = 203 s). Top-4 saves about 0 bytes in prefill. (3) FLOP split: expert weights 480 slices x 2.7 MB = 1.3 GB vs 1.9 GB dense, so experts are about 40% of the 12 GFLOP. Top-10->4 removes 0.6x0.4 = 24% of FLOPs, giving 1.3x compute, not 2.2x (the claim ignores that dense is fixed, which it admits, then still says 1.8-2.2). (4) GPU dense offload: only helps if the GPU can take compute; the experts still stream in, so prefill stays I/O-bound. (5) Where it does bite is DECODE (the answer never claims it): I ran the three Qwen3-30B traces truncated to the first k router ids (assumed score-ordered), LRU at fixed 2.1 footprints of the full k=8 cache (806 entries): misses per token (of 384 full) db 170.1 -> 70.9 (k=4) -> 48.3 (k=3); story 153.1 -> 63.0 -> 43.4; code 175.9 -> 78.6 -> 53.1. So bytes per token fall 2.2-2.4x for half the experts. For 125B top-10->4 (480->192 slices): bytes about 0.36-0.4x, compute ceiling 12 -> about 9.2 GFLOP => about 6.0 tok/s. At 8 GB with explicit 4 MiB reads+LRU: serial 2.18 -> about 1/(0.19+0.17)=2.8 tok/s (1.3x); overlap 4.16 -> capped at 6.0 (1.4x). Vs plain mmap (0.53) it is about 5x but that is the read-size win already counted, so it must not be stacked.
screened.arithmetic_error: Wrong baseline for the prefill compute (55 GFLOP/s decode rate used instead of the measured 311 GFLOP/s, 5.7x error). Ignores that 500-token prefill touches essentially every expert (98-100%), so I/O (29+ s) not compute (19 s) binds, and top-k reduction does not cut bytes. Overstates the FLOP saving (1.3x real vs 1.8-2.2x, because experts are only about 40% of FLOPs). Conflates TTFT with tok/s. Does not use the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling, which is raised only to about 6 by top-4. Quality cost +0.3-0.8 ppl is asserted without data.

screened.idea: Repack GGUF expert tensors at install time so each expert (gate, up, down, about 2.7 MB) is one contiguous 4 KiB-aligned extent, grouped per layer. At run time, read only the routed experts with aligned O_DIRECT (F_NOCACHE on macOS) reads into preallocated aligned buffers. This bypasses the mmap page-fault path (0.34 GB/s) and moves to the large-read regime (2.4 GB/s at 4 MiB).
screened.claimed_multiplier: claims array [1.4, 4.0, 7.0, 100.0]; idea says it 'lifts both prompt and decode' by removing the 0.34 GB/s fault-path ceiling
screened.arithmetic:
Not run (no trace analysis needed; pure arithmetic from FEED.md CORRECTED FACTS). Bytes per token = (1-hit) x 480 x 2.7 MB = 1.30 GB at hit 0. Compute ceiling is 4.57 tok/s, so 0.219 s/token of compute.
8 GB, hit 0.56 (LRU, 2.1 footprints), so 0.57 GB/token: mmap at 0.34 GB/s = 1.68 s IO, serial 0.53 tok/s, overlap 0.59. Explicit 4 MiB reads at 2.38 GB/s = 0.24 s IO, serial 2.18, overlap 4.16. Ratio 4.1x serial / 7.0x overlap. This reproduces the 4.0 and 7.0 claims, so 4-7x is the read-size gain and is already in our table. The 1.4 is the unrelated madvise decode-window number (wall-clock 1.09x). The 100 is withdrawn.
Read size matters: a 2.7 MB expert is about 3x 0.9 MB tensors. At 1.56 GB/s (1 MiB) the 8 GB row is about 1.2x lower. A contiguous 2.7 MB read lands between 1.56 and 2.4 GB/s (about 2.2).
Prefill: the full 69 GB is read at 2.4 GB/s = 29 s vs 203 s at 0.34 GB/s, so about 7x on load-bound prefill. Compute at 311 GFLOP/s is about 26 tok/s, so prefill stays read-bound and the gain applies there. The review's gap that prefill is unaddressed is wrong in direction, but the gain is capped by 69 GB / 2.4 GB/s = 29 s minimum.
16 GB (about 10 GB cache = 7.7 footprints, hit about 0.95, 0.065 GB/token): mmap 0.19 s IO, serial 2.4 tok/s; explicit 0.027 s, serial 4.0 tok/s. About 1.6x. My estimate, not measured.
32 GB (about 28 GB cache, hit about 0.97+): both near the 4.57 ceiling, about 1.1-1.2x. My estimate.
screened.arithmetic_error: (1) 'A few large reads per layer' is wrong for scattered experts. The 10 routed experts of 512 are not adjacent, so a single read per layer would pull about 1.4 GB. The gain comes from 10 independent 2.7 MB reads at queue depth, not from layer batching. (2) The 100x ignores the 4.57 tok/s compute ceiling and the 7x bandwidth ratio (2.38/0.34). (3) The 1.4 mixes a decode-window madvise ratio (wall-clock 1.09x) with this idea. (4) The 4-7x is vs mmap, not vs our best path; vs our best path (explicit large reads + LRU) the multiplier is 1.0x, because this idea IS that path. (5) Serial and overlap are different numbers (4.1x vs 7.0x); the overlap number needs a prefetch pipeline that does not exist yet.

screened.arithmetic: Ran python3 -I on the three qwen3-30b traces (299/249/249 tokens, footprint 384 accesses per token). Fraction of a token's experts already present in the previous token: db 0.425, story 0.455, code 0.417. LRU hit at 1 / 2 / 3 footprints: db 0.301/0.540/0.684, story 0.326/0.585/0.734, code 0.292/0.522/0.640. Throughput with 1.3 GB per token and no hits, plus 1/4.57 s of compute: 4 MiB reads at 2.4 GB/s give 0.54 s of I/O, serial 1.31 tok/s, overlap 1.85. 1 MiB reads at 1.56 GB/s give 0.83 s, serial 0.95, overlap 1.20. screened.arithmetic_error: (1) The 7-100x claim is withdrawn in FEED.md. (2) It uses mmap at 0.34 GB/s as the baseline but no cache, so the gain comes entirely from read size (0.34 to 2.4 GB/s = 7x raw bandwidth), and the 7x equals the raw ratio, not tok/s, because compute (0.22 s) is not counted. (3) The 2.4 GB/s figure is for 4 MiB reads, but experts are 3 tensors of about 0.9 MB. At that size the rate is 1.3-1.56 GB/s, so 4 MiB needs a re-laid-out file. (5) "No cache wins below one footprint" ignores the 0.42-0.45 overlap with the previous token: keeping only the previous token's slab (one footprint) cuts bytes by 42%, giving about 1.7x more tok/s on I/O-bound reads for free. It builds a per-layer greedy co-activation chain order and counts reads per token-layer (a read = a maximal run of adjacent expert slots). Identity (stock) layout: 7.48 / 7.58 / 7.54 reads per layer (db/story/code) for 8 experts, so mean run length 1.06. Order learned on the OTHER two prompts and tested on the held-out one: 5.77 / 6.21 / 6.06 reads, run length 1.39 / 1.29 / 1.32. Order learned on the same trace it is scored on (in-sample, not valid): 4.5 / 4.4 / 4.7 reads, run length 1.77 / 1.81 / 1.70. For comparison, simply merging reads across gaps of 1 or 3 slots, with no reorder, gives run length 1.12-1.13 / 1.25-1.26. So the held-out reorder yields about 1.3x longer reads, i.e. 0.9 MB -> about 1.2 MB per tensor read (or 2.7 -> about 3.5 MB if the three tensors are interleaved per expert). On our disk curve (1 MiB 1.56 GB/s, 4 MiB 2.4 GB/s) 1.3x longer reads is worth about 1.1-1.2x in disk rate, not 7x. Reorder also cannot touch the 512-expert, 10-active geometry in a way that clusters: on the 128-expert/top-8 trace, 8 reads of 7.5 collapse by only 20-23% with transferable ordering. In the 125B, with 512 experts and 10 picked, adjacency is rarer, so I expect the gain to be the same or smaller (not measured). Also the model ignores the cache: with a hit rate of 0.56 at 8 GB only the missing experts are read, and misses are a random subset of the token's experts, so they are less likely to be adjacent still. The compute ceiling 4.57 tok/s caps everything: at 8 GB our best path is 2.18 serial / 4.16 overlap tok/s, so even a perfect +20% disk rate gives at most 2.18 -> ~2.5 serial (+15%) and 4.16 -> 4.57 (+10%).

ranked.summary:
22 screenings merge into 8 surviving candidates plus 7 dropped items. Every screener recomputed the multiplier against our best path (explicit large reads plus LRU), not against mmap, and nearly all of the headline 3x to 100x claims collapsed to about 1.0x to 1.9x. The remaining gains are:
- A GPU tier, which needs hardware that does not match small-RAM PCs.
- A compute-side small-batch speculation gain that has not been measured.
- Quality-for-speed knobs, which are accuracy-gated and mostly help at 8 GB only.
No candidate meets all three revolutionary criteria. Every screener also found published prior art. The one partly-known item is the co-activation GGUF repack, and mbolt already ships it.

candidates.why_ranked_here: Smallest positive residual (about 1.1x), and already built by someone else.

dropped: Standalone expert-major lookahead/union batching as an I/O saver (speed#0, #1, #4; I/O half of #5 and families_problems#7): dropped because the union saving is the same temporal locality the LRU already captures. Simulated bytes per accepted token are 1.0x at best and 1.3-2.7x worse than LRU k=1 at 2.1 and 4 footprints. The 2.2x holds only at acceptance alpha=1 against an uncached 1.3 GB/token baseline.

Confidence-gated emit of the draft token without calling the big model (speed#5, second half): dropped because the output becomes the draft model's on about 60% of tokens (large unmeasured quality loss), the skipped position still needs KV backfill that reloads the same experts, and the 11 tok/s counts compute only.

No-cache per-token pread of a 1.3 GB slab (families_problems#1, problems#4): dropped because it is our best path with the cache removed. It runs at 0.60x / 0.44x of explicit reads plus LRU at 8 GB, 0.55x of plain mmap at 16 GB and 0.27x at 32 GB, because it throws away the page-cache hits. Adjacent-run merging saves only 5-6% of reads, so the required 25% byte cut is impossible. Only previous-token slab reuse (about 42% hit for one footprint) is worth keeping, folded into candidate 5.

Multi-sequence or lock-step batching across prompts (families_problems#2, problems#3): dropped because measured cross-prompt expert sharing is 1.06x for two streams and 1.12x for three. Aggregate gain is about 1.07x at K=8, 1.35x at K=32, 1.75x at K=64 and 2.7x at K=128, while per-user speed falls to 0.04-0.08 tok/s and KV for 128 contexts does not fit. It does not serve a single-user small-RAM PC.

Static pin of 24-26 GB of hot experts, with or without a routing bias (speed#10, static-pin half of speed#8): dropped because pin hit is at or below same-capacity LRU on all three traces (0.81-0.92 vs 0.89-0.94 at 36%). Net 0.6-0.75x of the best path at 8 GB, where 26 GB does not fit. The 24 GB pin needs a 32 GB machine, where LRU is already near the compute ceiling.

Prefill-only top-k cap (speed#11) and the GPU-offloaded-dense prefill claim (speed#13): dropped because 500 tokens touch 98-100% of experts at any k, so bytes barely fall (1.1-1.2x; 1.3-1.4x even at window W=64). Prefill compute is about 19 s at 311 GFLOP/s, and published prefill speedups are 1.15-1.55x. Decode-side top-k survives as candidate 3.

Fine-tuning the 125B router for temporal stickiness (speed#6, training half): dropped because no 125B training capability or data exists. The claim of 64 of 512 experts per prefill is far below natural routing (55-70% of experts touched at 249 tokens), and ReMoE already published it. The training-free bias survives as candidate 6.
arithmetic_errors_found: Union saving mis-sized as 17x: families and speed#4/#5 quote 17x (1.3 GB x 8 / 17 = 0.59 GB), which contradicts our own union table. The k=8 union is 29.1 of 64 draws (0.455), a 2.2x best-case byte saving, and only at alpha=1 and against an uncached baseline. Per accepted token it falls to 0.9-1.15x versus uncached at alpha 0.7-0.8, with break-even at alpha >= 0.75 (speed#0, #4, #5).

Wrong baseline, with the union saving double-counted against the LRU: bytes are compared with the uncached 1.3 GB/token (or mmap 2-4 tok/s) instead of explicit reads plus LRU, which already captures the same temporal overlap (speed#0, #1, #4, #5, #7, #8, #10, #12 and others).

Divisor of 8 assumes all drafts are accepted. Expected tokens per verify is (1-a^k)/(1-a), for example 2.4 at a=0.6 and 4.2 at a=0.8 for k=8. Rejected drafts still load their experts, and trace unions use true tokens, so they are optimistic (speed#0, #1, #4).

Prefill compute used the 55 GFLOP/s decode rate: 6 TFLOP / 55 GFLOP/s = 109 s is wrong; the measured prefill rate is about 311 GFLOP/s, giving about 19 s. The 'compute binds, so only 2.5x' conclusion is therefore wrong (speed#9, speed#13, speed#6; the 25 s TTFT in speed#6 mixes compute and I/O).

Straw-man prefill baseline: 650 GB (500 x 1.3 GB, per-token loading) versus 69 GB. Batched prefill never loads per token, and llama.cpp mul_mat_id at ubatch 512 already groups by expert, so only 50-69 GB is read in any scheme (speed#2, speed#9). Also 69 GB / 2.4 GB/s = 29 s uses the 4 MiB rate; at the real 0.9 MB tensor size (1.56 GB/s) it is about 44 s, and it assumes 100% expert coverage (traces suggest about 0.52-0.70 at 128-249 decode tokens, with 0.75-0.95 projected for a 500-token prompt).

Expert slice size wrong: 0.9 MB used instead of an expert of about 2.7 MB (three 0.9 MB tensors). This is a 3x byte understatement; 278 x 2.7 MB = 0.75 GB at 1.56 GB/s gives about 2.1 tok/s, not 6.2 (speed#12). The idea in speed#10 also used 0.9 MB and '69/512'.

Compute cut from top-k reduction overstated: 12 GFLOP/token is about 60% dense (1.9 GB, about 3.5B params) and about 40% experts. Cutting 10 to 6 removes about 16% of FLOPs (1.18x, ceiling 5.4 tok/s, not 7.6); cutting 10 to 4 removes about 24% (1.3x), not the claimed 1.65-2.2x (speed#3, speed#13, speed#11).

Byte and compute factors multiplied or added into a tok/s figure although throughput is min(compute, I/O) or a serial sum; 2.87x on bytes holds only with an empty cache (speed#3). Also 4.4-8.8 tok/s (speed#0), 5-8 tok/s (speed#6) and 5-10 tok/s (speed#11) all exceed the 4.57 ceiling (or about 6 for k=4). 11 tok/s (speed#5) counts compute only, ignoring I/O on the 40% of tokens still sent to the big model.
Model size: 34 GB for mixed 2/3/4-bit experts is wrong. Q2_K is about 2.6 bpw (about 42 GB) and a 2/3/4 mix is about 3 bpw (about 48 GB); only IQ2-class (about 2.06 bpw) reaches 33-34 GB (speed#7).

Cache hit conflated with other quantities: 40% reuse is quoted for a 6-10% pin but applied to a 24 GB (36%) set (speed#10); 42% previous-token reuse was used as the 20 GB cache hit rate when LRU gives about 0.85 there and static hot lists give only 0.44-0.70 (speed#12); 0.55 prefetch precision treated as coverage (speed#1).

Disk-rate ratio treated as speedup: the '7x' is 2.38/0.34 = 7.0 (and '100x' has no derivation), not tok/s, because 0.219 s of compute per token is ignored. It is also the read-size effect already in our best path, so it is not extra on top of explicit reads (problems#0, #4, #5, families_problems#1, #6). The 1.41 cited is the madvise decode-window ratio (wall-clock 1.09x, n=3), not a result of the idea (problems#0, families_problems#7).

The 2.4 GB/s read rate applies to 4 MiB reads; experts are 0.9 MB tensors unless re-laid-out, giving about 1.3-1.56 GB/s, and a 2.7 MB run interpolates to about 2.2 (problems#0, #4, #5, families_problems#1, speed#2). 'A few large reads per layer' is wrong for scattered experts (a single read per layer would pull about 1.4 GB), and adjacent-run merging helps only 5-6% of reads (problems#0, problems#4).

Aggregate throughput reported as per-user tok/s: with K concurrent prompts each user gets 1/K or less (0.04-0.08 tok/s at K=32-128), and the 6x/100x claims assume near-identical expert sets while measured sharing is 1.06-1.12x. Unique experts grow as 512(1-(1-10/512)^K) (families_problems#2, problems#3).

Scale mismatch: Qwen3-30B traces (128 experts, top-8, union 29/64 of 8k draws) were applied to the 125B (512 experts, top-10), where the 'of 64' text and the union fractions differ; the 24 GB 'small GPU' (speed#12) is not a small-RAM-PC component.

Compute ceiling handled inconsistently: speed#5 says the 4.57 tok/s ceiling does not bind a verify block (about 26 tok/s at 311 GFLOP/s), while speed#0, #4 and families_problems#7 treat batch-8 GFLOP/s as unmeasured and likely far below prefill (about 2 tokens per expert). This is flagged as an open measurement, not settled.

Hot-set premise: the claim that reuse is 'same-prompt' ignores that cross-prompt hot lists transfer at only 5-21%, and the 64-of-512 prefill expert claim is contradicted by 55-70% natural coverage at 249 tokens (speed#6, speed#10).
ranked.honest_headline: None of the 22 ideas qualifies as a revolutionary candidate. No candidate reaches 3x over our best path (explicit large reads plus LRU) on a realistic small-RAM machine. The best are about 2-2.6x for a 24 GB-VRAM GPU tier (hardware that does not fit the target), up to about 1.9x serial at 8 GB for top-k plus requant (accuracy-gated), and an unproven speculation compute upper bound that other screeners consider unrealistic. Every one has published prior art, and none is novel: the only partly-known item (co-activation GGUF repack) is already shipped as mbolt and is worth about 1.1x. The 3x to 100x headline claims were measured against plain mmap, an uncached baseline or a misattributed disk-rate ratio, and drop to about 1.0x once the LRU and the 4.57 tok/s compute ceiling are applied. The real wins left are engineering ones: build the explicit-read repack path (4-7x over mmap at 8 GB), then make the cheap measurements. Those are the 2.7 MB read rate, small-batch GFLOP/s and OLMoE perplexity at lower k.
